[p.7] Understanding Website Access and Traffic Sources Users visit websites using domain names. An example is api.mysite.com. The Domain Name System (DNS) helps translate these names into IP addresses. DNS is usually a paid service from third-party providers, not hosted on our servers. When a user requests a website, their browser or mobile app receives an Internet Protocol (IP) address. For example, the IP address returned could be 15.125.23.214. After getting the IP address, the browser sends requests using Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) directly to the web server. The web server then sends back HTML pages or a JSON response that the browser uses to display content. Traffic Sources to Your Web Server Traffic to your web server primarily comes from two sources: web applications and mobile applications. Web application: This uses server-side languages like Java or Python to manage business logic and storage. It also uses client-side languages like HTML and JavaScript for displaying content. Mobile application: This uses the HTTP protocol to communicate with the web server. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is often used as the response format for APIs because it is simple to read. For example, to get information about a user, an API request might look like this: GET /users/12 to retrieve the user object for id = 12.

[p.8] Database As the number of users grows, one server isn't enough. We need several servers: one for handling web and mobile traffic, and another for managing the database. This setup allows us to scale them separately. Which databases to use? You can pick between a traditional relational database and a non-relational database. Let's look at their differences. Relational databases, also known as relational database management systems (RDBMS) or SQL databases, include popular options like MySQL, Oracle database, and PostgreSQL. These databases store data in tables and rows. You can use SQL to perform join operations across different tables. Non-relational databases, or NoSQL databases, include popular ones like CouchDB, Neo4j, Cassandra, HBase, and Amazon DynamoDB. These databases fall into four categories: key-value stores, graph stores, column stores, and document stores. Generally, non-relational databases do not support join operations. For most developers, relational databases are the preferred choice. They have existed for over 40 years and have a strong track record. However, if relational databases don't meet your needs, it's important to consider non-relational options. Non-relational databases might be best if: Your application needs very low latency. Your data is unstructured, or you do not have any connected data. You just need to serialize and deserialize data (like JSON, XML, YAML, etc.). You need to store a vast amount of data.

[p.9] Vertical Scaling vs Horizontal Scaling Vertical scaling, called "scale up," is when you add more power like CPU and RAM to your existing servers. This means you're making a single server stronger. Horizontal scaling, known as "scale out," involves adding more servers to your group of resources. This increases your overall capacity by having more machines work together. Vertical scaling works well when traffic is low. It's simple and easy to manage. However, it has serious drawbacks. Vertical scaling has a hard limit. You cannot keep adding CPU and memory to one server indefinitely. Vertical scaling lacks failover and redundancy. If one server fails, the entire website or app will go down. Horizontal scaling is often better for applications that need to handle a large number of users. This is due to the limits found in vertical scaling. In a typical design, users connect directly to the web server. If that server goes offline, users cannot access the website. If too many users try to connect at the same time and the server reaches its load limit, they may see slow responses or fail to connect. Using a load balancer helps solve these issues. A load balancer distributes user traffic across multiple servers, improving reliability and performance.
